summary:
Ankara stands within Turkey's national framework, and the exposure points identified for a trans visitor lie inside the country rather than at the border. The institutions driving the documented hostility operate in Ankara: Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft "11th Judicial Package" would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years' prison, and to punish participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, trans people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years, and courts could order pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft. Whether the package has since passed is unresolved in the sources.

Kaos GL's annual report, "The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People", finds that hostility toward LGBTI+ people has become explicit state policy centred on the presidency, with the Ministry of Family as the implementing ministry. Broadcasts have been censored, artistic events cancelled or banned, and an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members. The report documents six violations of the right to life over the year, three recorded as hate-motivated, with trans people the most affected, and a sharp rise in torture and ill-treatment violations to 89 from 51 the previous year. The state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so these figures rest on civil-society monitoring alone.

For a trans visitor, the practical exposure is street-level identity checking and, if detained, custody conditions. Detainees are held in facilities organised by registered sex rather than gender identity, and Turkish prisons subject LGBTI+ detainees to arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation and restricted healthcare. No policy or staff training exists to identify LGBTI+ needs, complaints are ineffective and can provoke further violence, and transfers are frequent. Ankara's Sincan Women's Prison is the site of one such case: on 1 December 2025 the transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell, with rights groups demanding an independent investigation and changes to detention practices affecting transgender prisoners.

Protection machinery is thin. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and no direct discrimination protection for gender identity. If medication is needed during a stay, hormone replacement therapy is not covered by the government healthcare system, so trans visitors must obtain and pay for it privately.
tangentialFactors:
The draft judicial package sits within a broader authoritarian drift, with the Erdoğan government repeatedly using "the family" and "public morals" framing to legitimise stigmatisation. Kaos GL's framing of 2025 as "The Year of the Family" indicates that official rhetoric and administrative action are aligned rather than incidental.

The absence of official hate-crime statistics means that monitoring by organisations such as Kaos GL is the only available count, and any comparison across years or jurisdictions rests on that single civil-society dataset.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the leaked "11th Judicial Package" has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources; the inventory records it as a draft opposed by fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association as of 29 October 2025.

The Kaos GL figures for right-to-life violations and torture or ill-treatment are civil-society counts, since the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics; no independent denominator or per-capita comparison is sourced here.
